newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Murdoch scores sports triumphs in Australia, Asia.
newsitem.headline: Murdoch scores sports triumphs in Australia, Asia.

text.p: Rupert Murdoch moved closer to becoming a global force in sports programming on Friday after winning approval for his rebel rugby league concept and announcing a new Asian television partnership.

The Australian offshoot of Murdoch's News Corp Ltd won legal approval to launch its Super League tournament, which will form a key part of his local Foxtel pay television network venture. Super League represents a direct market challenge to the teams now controlled by the Australian Rugby League.
Murdoch has already spent A$270 million (US$214 million) on Super League and media analysts were concerned that a loss in Friday's court ruling would mean the money had been wasted.

Super League is also likely to feature on News Corp's planned Asian sports programming joint venture with ESPN, the sports channel of U.S. television and film giant Walt Disney, which was announced in Hong Kong on Friday.

ESPN and STAR TV, News Corp's satellite TV broadcaster based in Hong Kong, plan to beam sports programming services throughout Asia, except for Japan, Australia and New Zealand, where both parties have separate pre-existing ventures.
The ESPN sports deal follows News Corp's global sports joint venture with U.S. cable TV giant Tele-Communications Inc in May.
News Corp has vast global television interests through its Fox Televsion Network in the United States, a 40 percent interest in UK-based BSkyB and its wholly owned STAR TV in Asia.

The Super League victory was hailed by Rupert Murdoch's eldest son Lachlan, who is managing director of local offshoot News Ltd, as an important victory for Foxtel in its battle with fellow pay TV group Optus Vision, which is backed by billionaire media baron Kerry Packer.

"I think it is a win not only for Super League and for supporters of rugby league in general and the players and also for Foxtel obviously," Lachlan Murdoch told reporters in a news conference after the Federal Court decision.
He left the door open for the potential sale of television rights with Packer's top-ranked commercial television network Channel Nine.
"We will have more rugby league now on both free-to-air and pay television through Foxtel," Murdoch said.
Asked if News would sell the free-to-air rights to Packer's Nine Network television station, he replied "If they have the cash to put up...we will listen to them, absolutely."
Packer's Nine Network currently broadcasts the Australian Rugby League (ARL) competition and stands to lose the most from Friday's court ruling, analysts said.
The ARL tournament is also beamed on Optus Vision.

But News Corp did not entirely win the day. The court ruled that News Corp would have to pay damages to the ARL, the local ruling body, for the disruption caused by its attempt to create Super League. News Ltd chairman Ken Cowley said he could not say how much News would have to pay.
